So if you’re allergic to one, you may not be allergic to the others. * Some skin wounds can be severe and shouldn’t be treated at home. Rather, they require medical attention from a healthcare professional. When you get a cut or scrape, you may find yourself reaching for the first-aid kit to clean, bandage, and care for the wound. One common product found in first-aid kits is an antibiotic ointment, such as Polysporin (bacitracin / polymyxin B), Neosporin (bacitracin / neomycin / polymyxin B), or bacitracin. These products help prevent or treat infection. All of these ointments are available over the counter (OTC), so you can buy them without a prescription. But what are the differences between these antibiotics ointments? And if you’re considering purchasing one to keep at home, which one should you choose? It’s also helpful to know when to use an antibiotic ointment and when it’s best to avoid one. Read on to learn what you need to know about Polysporin, Neosporin, and bacitracin. Antibiotic ointments are medications that are applied topically — on the skin — to help kill bacteria. Healthcare professionals often use them to treat minor skin injuries such as scrapes, cuts, or burns. Using antibiotic ointments is one part of caring for skin wounds. It’s also important to clean and sometimes bandage an injury. Antibiotic ointments don’t help with pain, inflammation, or itching. But they do help treat and prevent infection. These symptoms can happen with infections, so treating an infection can help relieve this discomfort. Infected wounds may become more painful, red in color, or swollen. And infections can lead to serious health consequences if left untreated. The OTC antibiotic ointments Polysporin, Neosporin, and bacitracin are useful for minor skin injuries, such as cuts, scrapes, and burns. Below is some basic information to know about each of these OTC antibiotic ointments. It’s important to keep in mind that cost may vary, especially if you’re purchasing a generic or store-brand version. Instructions on how to use Polysporin, Neosporin, and bacitracin are the same for each product. First, clean the skin injury area with soap and water. Then, apply a small amount (about the size of the tip of your finger) on the wound 1 to 3 times daily. Cover the area with a bandage if needed. You should apply the ointment after cleaning the wound. If a wound doesn’t easily stay closed with a bandage or other basic dressing, you should seek the help of a healthcare professional. You may need stitches, sutures, or another treatment. > Good to know: Neomycin is a common cause of contact dermatitis, a type of allergic skin reaction. This ingredient is found in Neosporin, but not in Polysporin or bacitracin. If you have a history of contact dermatitis or sensitive skin, it may be a good idea to avoid using antibiotic ointments that contain neomycin. OTC antibiotic ointments are more effective at preventing infections than not using an antibiotic. But there’s very little research that shows differences in how well particular products work. So, choosing the best antibiotic ointment for you will depend on your preferences, allergies, and recommendations (if any) from a healthcare professional. Neosporin contains three active ingredients, whereas Polysporin contains two and bacitracin contains one. Keep in mind, having more active ingredients doesn’t necessarily mean the ointment will work better. For some wounds, bacitracin may work just as well as Polysporin or Neosporin. Your healthcare professional can let you know if your wound requires treatment with more than one antibiotic. It’s also good to keep any allergies and sensitivities in mind when choosing an antibiotic ointment. For example, if you’re allergic or sensitive to polymyxin B, then bacitracin would be the best choice. That’s because Neosporin and Polysporin both contain polymyxin B. And if you’re allergic or sensitive to neomycin, either Polysporin or bacitracin would be acceptable. fetched_contents.text: How to tell if a wound is healing or infected Last updated November 6, 2025 Your body is set up to start healing as soon as it’s cut or injured. But sometimes, for any number of reasons, the body doesn’t do exactly what it’s supposed to when it’s supposed to. Sometimes a wound takes a long time to heal or gets infected and stops the healing process altogether. It’s important to pay attention to the stages of wound healing so you know whether your wound is going in the right direction. Alyssa Smolen, APRN, is a wound care expert at OSF HealthCare who shared how to tell if a wound is healing or infected. The wound healing process A typical wound starts to heal right away following a four-step process: 1. Hemostasis- The body knows when it’s been wounded and focuses on stopping the bleeding first. This process can happen within seconds or minutes of getting a wound. Hemostasis also helps get the body ready for the second stage of healing. 2. Inflammation- Your body’s defense system sends white blood cells to the wound to help clear out bacteria and debris. You might see experience some redness, swelling, warmth or pain. 3. Proliferation- Once the wound is stabilized, it goes into rebuild mode. The body sends oxygen-rich blood cells and collagen to the wound, which helps the body to form new skin. It may look red and raised at this stage. 4. Maturation- Maturation is the stage of healing when a scar softens, flattens and fades. You’ll notice your wound looking more like the skin that was once there. During this stage, the body is strengthening the area. Depending on the severity of the wound, maturation may take a year or more to fully complete. Signs of wound healing “How long it takes for a cut to heal can vary depending on the wound. If you notice your cut isn’t healing within a month, it’s considered a chronic wound and it’s time to talk to a wound care specialist,” Alyssa said. Keeping track of your wound and the stage of healing it’s in can help to identify whether it’s a healing or non-healing wound. Sign of healing include: * Clotting blood at the wound * Swelling * Scarring How to heal a wound that won’t close Open wounds and wounds that are slow to heal should be looked at by a health care provider. “If your wound is non-healing or slow-healing, are considered chronic wounds. There are many options your provider may suggest, including oral prescription medication to improve blood flow, topical prescriptions to help clear up any infection, wound debridement, hyperbaric oxygen treatment or therapy to reduce swelling,” Alyssa said. Wound debridement is a process of removing dead or infected tissue from the wound. This helps a wound to heal faster and ensures that healthy tissue can grow. “If you have a wound that continuously bleeds or has shown no signs of closing after a day, it’s important to talk to a health care provider,” Alyssa said. Signs a wound is infected Signs of wound infection should be taken seriously. * Fever and chills- Any time a fever is present, your body is likely fighting off an infection. The key red flags for infection in a minor cut are **increased pain or bleeding**, **discolored, green, yellow, or brown liquid or pus**, **foul-smelling discharge**, **fever and chills**, **increased redness**, and **swelling** that worsens over time [N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-F3]. The OSF HealthCare source also emphasizes that a wound should be treated as a non-healing wound if it shows no signs of closing after a day or if it is slow to heal, and that chronic wounds or non-infected wounds are not appropriate for antibiotic ointments [N3-F3]. The Cleveland Clinic wound infection source likewise notes that symptoms such as pus draining from the site, redness, pain, or heat are symptoms of a surgical wound infection, and that prompt care is needed if the cut is deep or redness/swelling increases [N3-R4][N3-R5].

A doctor visit is reasonable if the wound shows any of these signs: **the cut isn’t healing within a month**, **it is a chronic wound**, **it continuously bleeds**, **it has shown no signs of closing after a day**, or if the wound **does not improve within about 1 week or is getting worse** [N3-F3][N3-R5]. The OSF HealthCare article also states that open wounds and wounds that are slow to heal should be seen by a healthcare provider, and that non-healing wounds may require prescription treatments such as oral medication, topical prescriptions, debridement, hyperbaric oxygen, or therapy for swelling [N3-F3]. In practical terms, this means the patient should not delay medical attention if the wound is not improving or if the redness, pain, or drainage worsens.

After initial care, the wound should be monitored for any new or worsening symptoms. The OSF HealthCare source recommends keeping the wound **moist and covered**, changing dressings, and keeping it clean with warm water and gentle soap [N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic and NHS sources also support cleaning with soap and water, rinsing with warm water, and using gauze or cloth to wipe away from the wound [N1-R1][N1-R4]. ## Final integrated answer

The short answer is: **yes, it’s safe to clean the cut, cover it with a bandage, and apply an over-the-counter antibacterial ointment only after that, but the best first step is simply to clean and cover the wound properly** [N1-R1][N1-R4][N3-F3].

### 1) What the patient should do immediately after cleaning the cut

The branch reports show a clear first-aid sequence for a small, non-bleeding cut: **clean the wound with soap and water, rinse with warm water, and then cover it with a clean bandage or dressing** [N1-R1][N1-R4][N3-F3]. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes cleaning with soap and water or warm water and gentle soap, then wiping away from the wound [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The wound should then be covered with a dressing or bandage, not left uncovered unnecessarily [N3-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5].

So the immediate steps are:

1. **Rinse the wound with water** [N1-R1].
2. **Clean the skin around the wound with soap and water** [N1-R4].
3. **Apply a clean bandage or dressing** [N1-R4][N3-F3].
4. **Change the bandage regularly** [N4-R3][N4-R5].

The branch reports also note that **removing wound coverings too soon can compromise healing** and that bandages should be changed as needed, ideally twice a day in the early stages [N4-R1][N4-R3]. That means the patient should not keep the bandage on for days without checking, but also should not worry about a bandage “messing up” the wound if it is clean and not causing discomfort [N4-R3][N4-R4].

### 2) When to use an antibacterial ointment versus when it’s not needed

The evidence supports using an over-the-counter antibacterial ointment **only when there is a real risk of infection or when infection is suspected**, not as a routine first-aid step for a clean, small cut [N3-F3][N2-F2]. The branch report on antibiotic ointment explains that these products can be helpful early on to prevent infection, but they are **not appropriate for chronic wounds or non-infected wounds** [N3-F3]. The GoodRx review adds that OTC antibiotic ointments are useful for minor skin injuries with an increased risk of contamination and should be reserved primarily for preventing infection in such wounds [N2-F2].

So the patient should **not apply ointment immediately after cleaning** the wound as a default step [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The branch report says the ointment is useful mainly when there is a risk of infection or when infection is suspected, but it is not needed for a clean, shallow cut [N3-F3][N2-F2]. If the patient is **not allergic to antibiotic creams**, that still does not mean they should use ointment immediately; the evidence supports using it only after cleaning and covering the wound, and only if needed later [N1-R1][N1-R4][N3-F3].

### 3) When to worry about infection and when to seek care

For a minor cut with no bleeding, no redness, and no discharge, the evidence suggests that infection is **not a routine concern**, but it should still be monitored closely [N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-F3]. The branch report lists specific red flags for infection: **increased pain or bleeding**, **discolored, green, yellow, or brown liquid or pus**, **foul-smelling discharge**, **fever and chills**, **increased redness**, and **swelling** that worsens over time [N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-F3].

A doctor visit is reasonable if the wound shows any of these signs or if it **does not improve within about 1 week or is getting worse** [N3-F3][N3-R5]. The branch reports also say that wounds that are slow to heal or that show no signs of closing after a day should be seen by a healthcare provider [N3-F3]. In practical terms, the patient should not delay care if the wound looks worse over time or if any infection signs appear [N3-F3][N3-R5].

### 4) Best practical advice for the patient’s situation

Putting it all together, the best practical advice for the patient’s small shallow cut is:

- **Do not panic.** The cut is minor and the patient has already done the right first step: cleaning with soap and water [N1-R1][N1-R4].
- **Do clean it again if needed.** The evidence supports cleaning around the wound with soap and water and wiping away from the wound [N1-R4].
- **Do cover it with a bandage or dressing.** The evidence says wounds should be kept moist and covered, and that leaving wounds uncovered unnecessarily can be a misconception [N3-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5].
- **Do change the bandage regularly.** The branch reports suggest changing the dressing twice a day in the early stages and changing it daily if needed [N4-R3][N4-R5].
- **Do not apply ointment immediately after cleaning.** The evidence does not support applying ointment right after cleaning as a routine step; it is reserved for infection risk or suspected infection [N1-R1][N1-R4][N3-F3].
- **Do apply ointment only if needed later.** If the wound looks clean, not bleeding, and has no signs of infection, ointment is optional and should not be used as a default [N3-F3][N2-F2].
- **Do monitor the wound daily.** The branch reports emphasize checking for changes in color, warmth, swelling, drainage, and pain [N3-R3][N3-R4][N9].
- **Do seek care if anything worsens.** If the wound starts to bleed more, gets red, swollen, painful, or produces pus or foul-smelling discharge, the patient should see a doctor [N3-R3][N3-R5].

### 5) How to manage anxiety about bandage use versus no bandage

The branch reports show that the patient’s worry is reasonable, but it should be managed carefully. The evidence supports covering the wound as a standard practice because it reduces infection risk, not because the wound “needs” air [N3-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5]. The branch reports also note that bandages should be changed regularly and that removing coverings too soon can compromise healing [N4-R1][N4-R3]. So the patient should not worry about keeping the bandage on all day if it is clean and not causing discomfort; the better worry is keeping the wound covered and changing the dressing as needed [N4-R3][N4-R4].

At the same time, the evidence does not support leaving the wound uncovered for prolonged periods. The best approach is to **cover it, change the bandage regularly, and keep the wound moist and clean** [N3-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5]. If the patient is concerned about a bandage being “too tight,” the evidence also says not to wrap it too tightly, because that can restrict blood flow or cause discomfort [N6-R5].

### 6) Step-by-step care sequence for the patient’s situation

Here is a simple, step-by-step sequence that matches the evidence:

1. **Rinse the wound with water** [N1-R1].
2. **Clean the skin around the wound with soap and water** [N1-R4].
3. **Apply a clean bandage or dressing** [N1-R4][N3-F3].
4. **Change the bandage regularly** [N4-R3][N4-R5].
5. **Monitor daily for redness, swelling, pain, pus, or fever** [N3-R3][N3-R4][N9].
6. **Apply an over-the-counter antibacterial ointment only if needed later** [N3-F3][N2-F2].
7. **See a doctor if the wound worsens or does not improve** [N3-F3][N3-R5].

### 7) Bottom line for the spouse

The spouse can be reassured that this is a **minor injury** and that the patient has already taken the right steps by cleaning the cut with soap and water [N1-R1][N1-R4]. A bandage is safe and often helpful, but it should be changed regularly and not kept on too long without checking [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Antibacterial ointment is **not needed right away**, and the patient should use it only if there is a real concern about infection [N3-F3][N2-F2]. The most important thing is to **keep the wound clean, covered, and monitored**, and to see a doctor only if the wound worsens or shows signs of infection [N3-R3][N3-R5].

So the answer to the patient’s question is: **yes, it is safe to clean and cover the cut, and to use an over-the-counter antibacterial ointment only if needed later—but the best first step is simply to clean and cover properly** [N1-R1][N1-R4][N3-F3].

The OSF HealthCare source also emphasizes that a wound should be treated as a non-healing wound if it shows no signs of closing after a day or if it is slow to heal, and that chronic wounds or non-infected wounds are not appropriate for antibiotic ointments [N3-F3]. The Cleveland Clinic wound infection source likewise notes that symptoms such as pus draining from the site, redness, pain, or heat are symptoms of a surgical wound infection, and that prompt care is needed if the cut is deep or redness/swelling increases [N3-R4][N3-R5].

A doctor visit is reasonable if the wound shows any of these signs: **the cut isn’t healing within a month**, **it is a chronic wound**, **it continuously bleeds**, **it has shown no signs of closing after a day**, or if the wound **does not improve within about 1 week or is getting worse** [N3-F3][N3-R5]. The OSF HealthCare article also states that open wounds and wounds that are slow to heal should be seen by a healthcare provider, and that non-healing wounds may require prescription treatments such as oral medication, topical prescriptions, debridement, hyperbaric oxygen, or therapy for swelling [N3-F3]. In practical terms, this means the patient should not delay medical attention if the wound is not improving or if the redness, pain, or drainage worsens.

After initial care, the wound should be monitored for any new or worsening symptoms. The OSF HealthCare source recommends keeping the wound **moist and covered**, changing dressings, and keeping it clean with warm water and gentle soap [N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic and NHS sources also support cleaning with soap and water, rinsing with warm water, and using gauze or cloth to wipe away from the wound [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The wound should be checked regularly for changes in color, warmth, swelling, drainage, and pain, and the patient should seek care if any of these worsen [N3-F3][N3-R5]. The evidence does not support leaving the wound uncovered for long without a bandage, because it is best to keep wounds covered to reduce infection risk [N3-F3].

In short, the patient should treat this minor cut as a low-risk injury but remain alert for the specific infection signs listed above. If the wound looks clean, not bleeding, and has no redness or discharge, the risk is low, but monitoring is still important [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-F3].

So the immediate steps are:

1. **Rinse the wound with water** [N1-R1].
2. **Clean the skin around the wound with soap and water** [N1-R4].
3. **Apply a clean bandage or dressing** [N1-R4][N3-F3].
4. **Change the bandage regularly** [N4-R3][N4-R5].

The branch reports also note that **removing wound coverings too soon can compromise healing** and that bandages should be changed as needed, ideally twice a day in the early stages [N4-R1][N4-R3]. ### 2) When to use an antibacterial ointment versus when it’s not needed

The evidence supports using an over-the-counter antibacterial ointment **only when there is a real risk of infection or when infection is suspected**, not as a routine first-aid step for a clean, small cut [N3-F3][N2-F2]. ### 3) When to worry about infection and when to seek care

In practical terms, the patient should not delay care if the wound looks worse over time or if any infection signs appear [N3-F3][N3-R5].

- **Do not panic.** The cut is minor and the patient has already done the right first step: cleaning with soap and water [N1-R1][N1-R4].
